words_with_history.title: Orð með sögu
text: „Nú koma ragnarök!“ segir Óli á páskum, og hann hlær.
Um morguninn er myrkur á Hömrum. „Nú koma ragnarök, Óli?“ spyr Gamla-Manga, og Óli segir ekkert.
„Eru þetta ragnarök?“ spyr Siggi á hádegi. Enginn svarar.
Ragnarök eru í Völuspá, í bók afa. Þar er sólin svört.
words_with_history.note_en: Ragnarök is 'the fate (rök) of the powers (regin)': the end of the gods in Völuspá. Snorri often writes ragnarökkr, 'twilight of the powers' (rökkr, dusk), a different word, and Wagner's Götterdämmerung comes from it.

pronunciation_note.rule: In hljóð, initial hl- is a voiceless l: let air pass along the sides of the tongue without voicing. It is one consonant sound [l̥], not a separate h followed by an ordinary l.

grammar.title: Hvers? — sonur Bjarna, ljós dagsins
grammar.rule: Siggi er sonur Bjarna. Aska fellur á þak bæjarins. Ásta fer til Helgu.

tables.caption: sonur · dóttir
rows: Sigurður Bjarna·son (s099–s100) · Ásta Bjarna·dóttir (s103) · Helga Bjarna·dóttir (s107)

grammar.note_en:
The genitive (ef., eignarfall) is a case: a form of a noun, name or pronoun that marks a relationship. Its central use here is possession or belonging, like English “of” or “-’s”. Bók afa (s029) is “Grandad’s book”; rúm afa (s093, s095), “Grandad’s bed”; skór Bjarna (s075), “Bjarni’s shoes”; sonur Bjarna (s100), “Bjarni’s son”. The owner follows the thing owned. This relation need not be literal ownership: ljós dagsins (s040–s041) is “the light of day”, hurð bæjarins (s045) “the farm’s door”, and þak bæjarins (s051) “the farm’s roof”. Hvers? asks “whose?”: Hvers sonur er pabbi? (s108), “Whose son is Dad?”; Hvers sonur ert þú, afi? (s119), “Whose son are you, Grandad?”

There is no single genitive ending. Many strong masculine and neuter nouns take -s; other masculine nouns take -ar. Feminine nouns commonly take -ar, while weak feminine nouns take -u; weak masculine nouns commonly take -a. The genitive plural often ends in -a. These are patterns to recognise, not a rule for guessing every noun. A stem may change too: bær → bæjar, “farm → of a farm”; fé → fjár, “sheep / livestock → of sheep”; aska → ösku, “ash → of ash”. Afi → afa is “Grandad → Grandad’s”; Bjarni → Bjarna is “Bjarni → Bjarni’s”. In til Helgu (s036), “to Helga”, final -a becomes -u. These forms have already occurred in the story; consult the table when needed.

The suffixed definite article means “the”. In the genitive the article itself changes. A strong masculine or neuter -s genitive plus article -ins gives the familiar sequence -sins; an -ar genitive plus -ins gives -arins, as in bæjarins. Feminine definite forms show -arinnar or weak -unnar; plural forms show -anna. This does not mean attaching those letters to a nominative unchanged. Dagur has genitive dags; with the article it becomes dagsins, “of the day”. Hljóðsins (s036) is “of the sound”; myrkursins (s042), “of the darkness”; bæjarins (s045, s051), “of the farm”; fjárins (s066), “of the sheep / flock”. The masculine noun bær has genitive bæjar before the article; the result is bæjarins, not bærsins. Fé likewise has the irregular stem fjár. Sólarinnar (s132) means “of the sun”; öskunnar (s072), “of the ash”; skepnanna (s068), “of the animals”. Skónna (s046), “of the shoes”, is a plural form with a contracted article; compare skór, “shoes”, skóna, “the shoes” as an accusative, and skónna as a genitive. The table preserves these actual forms rather than inventing one uniform ending. Its nominative labels are familiar words, sometimes from earlier chapters; the references identify this chapter’s genitives.

An Icelandic patronymic is normally the father’s name in the genitive plus son, “son”, or dóttir, “daughter”. Bjarna·son therefore means “Bjarni’s son”, and Bjarna·dóttir means “Bjarni’s daughter”: Sigurður Bjarnason (s099), Ásta Bjarnadóttir (s103), and Helga Bjarnadóttir (s107). Jón → Jóns gives Jóns·son, “Jón’s son”, in Bjarni Jónsson (s109), and Jóns·dóttir, “Jón’s daughter”, in Þórunn’s name (s113). Einar → Einars gives Einars·dóttir, “Einar’s daughter”, in Guðrún Einarsdóttir (s116); Ásta hears Einars in s117, and afi says Ég heiti Einar (s118), “My name is Einar”. The story uses independent genitive Sigurðar (s122), while its established patronymic is Sigurðsson (s120), with the shorter shape Sigurðs-. Follow the family’s attested name rather than mechanically replacing the compound with the independent genitive just seen. Thus Einar Sigurðsson is the son of the older Sigurður; Siggi, also Sigurður, carries that older man’s given name (s122–s123). The middle dots in the table only display the parts; ordinary spelling joins them.

Icelanders are normally addressed by first name. A patronymic is not a family surname shared unchanged by every member: the children’s father is Bjarni Jónsson, while their mother is Guðrún Einarsdóttir. A woman keeps her own patronymic on marriage. Siggi and Ásta are familiar forms of the given names Sigurður and Ástríður (s099, s104); Margrét Sveinsdóttir is Manga’s full name (s126). The names appear in the case the sentence needs, just like other nouns: Bjarni is a subject; Bjarna marks the relationship in sonur Bjarna. Proper names are not exempt from case. The full names are reading support, not words to memorise or spell from gaps.

Three new prepositions require the genitive: til, “to”; án, “without”; vegna, “because of”. Ásta fer til Helgu (s036) means “Ásta goes to Helga”; Ég fer til fjárins (s066), “I am going to the sheep”; til skepnanna (s068), “to the animals”; Ekki án Óla (s067), “Not without Óli”. Vegna hljóðsins (s036) means “because of the sound”; vegna myrkursins (s042), “because of the darkness”; vegna öskunnar (s072), “because of the ash”. This case is required by the preposition; it does not mean that someone owns the sound or ash. Compare the familiar dative prepositions: hjá Helgu (s081), “with / beside Helga”; hjá kindunum (s071), “with the ewes”; frá Sigga (s135), “from Siggi”; af öskunni (s075), “from the ash”. Helgu happens to look the same in dative and genitive. Til tells us it is genitive, hjá that it is dative. Í baðstofunni (s038), “in the baðstofa”, and á túninu (s048), “on the homefield”, are dative locations. Í skóna (s044), “into the shoes / putting the shoes on”, instead uses the accusative; án skónna (s046), “without the shoes”, uses the genitive. No new dative shoe form is needed here.

Pronouns have genitive forms too. Dóttir hans (s103) means “his daughter”, referring to Bjarni; ætt okkar (s123), “our family / lineage”, includes afi and Siggi. Hans belongs with hann, “he”; okkar with við, “we”. Unlike an adjective describing a daughter, hans does not change to agree with dóttir. The genitive question form is hvers, “whose”. The genitive of hún is hennar, “her / hers”, but the story does not use it, so there is no new table cell or exercise for it. Nafn pabba míns (s123), “my father’s name”, has both pabba and míns in the genitive. Míns belongs to minn, “my”; the whole phrase tells whose name it is. Nú átt þú það (s123) means “now you own / have it”, the old name: átt is the second-person present of eiga, not a preposition.

The last table is a look-up aid at the end of Hluti 1, not a grid to fill in or recite. The four cases now divide the work. Nominative (nf., nefnifall) identifies a subject: askan in Hvaðan kemur askan? (s061), “Where does the ash come from?” Accusative (þf., þolfall) identifies the direct object of skoða: skoðar öskuna (s060), “looks at the ash”. Dative (þgf., þágufall) follows af in af öskunni (s075), “from the ash”, and marks an object after fylgja in fylgir honum (s018), “follows him”, Bjarni. Genitive (ef., eignarfall) follows vegna in vegna öskunnar (s072), “because of the ash”, and marks a relationship in rúm afa (s093), “Grandad’s bed”. In the afi row, afi (s032) is “Grandad” as subject; skoðar afa (s121) is “looks at Grandad”; hjá afa (s139), “beside Grandad”; rúm afa (s093), “Grandad’s bed”. Three cases of this weak noun look alike. In the pronoun row, hann (s055) is “it”, the stone, as subject; skoða hann (Kafli 9 s044), “look at him”, refers to Siggi as object; fylgir honum (s018), “follows him”, refers to Bjarni; dóttir hans (s103), “his daughter”, also refers to Bjarni. The antecedents differ because these are actual story occurrences, not one invented sentence. Case is a noun’s or pronoun’s job in its own sentence; identical spelling does not make two cases the same.
